cells.tense: You are standing in what the last stretch of change has actually produced.
cells.ask: Go through one thing the change produced and decide once — keep it or leave it — then act on that call today.
cells.core: Look around at what the last stretch actually made. Not the plan and not the story you tell about it — the stuff itself, what's here now, what arrived while you were living through it. You're the one who chooses what to carry out of this. That's not force. It's picking, deliberately, and you're doing it well.\n\nThe catch of being this good at it is that choosing well still costs something. You will leave things behind. Some things are already done with you, and letting them go cleanly is the other half of the call. Share the picking with someone before you finish — say what you're keeping and why, out loud, once.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one who decides what carries forward from this, and you do.
cells.verb: gathering what the change already grew
cells.place: where you choose what to carry forward

cells.tense: You will have already gathered it all before it has finished growing.
cells.ask: Leave one thing in place this week and tell the person closest to it that you're waiting.
cells.core: You're standing in a harvest that isn't ready and calling it late. You start counting what this will have produced before it's produced it — who gets credit, what gets kept, how it all reads once measured. Each pass through the books is another version of an end you can't write yet.\n\nWhat you miss is what already settled: the change itself, the way this chapter actually ended, the people it ended with. The gathering can hold until the thing is done. Let what's still growing finish out of your hands — not because you don't care, but because reaching in now is the one move that changes the crop.
cells.sheetLine: You're tallying a harvest that's still in the ground.

cells.tense: You stopped at the edge of what this produced, and the field is behind you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're ready to carry out of the last stretch, then take one visible step toward it this week.
cells.core: Something finished. You can feel where the edge was — the point past which this was done. You didn't walk out into it. You've stayed at the gate, doing the watching without the gathering, so what arrived just sits there.\n\nThat's not from laziness. Picking something up and calling it yours is a choice, and choice is where you've gone quiet. The feeling that would tell you 'yes, that one' is still moving in you; it just hasn't been pointed anywhere. When you engage with what you actually want, the direction comes with it. Pick the thing you'd pick if no one were watching. It doesn't have to be the whole field.
cells.sheetLine: The harvest is here and you've stopped reaching for it.

cells.tense: The gathering has already happened, and you are calling it waiting.
cells.ask: Write down one choice you've already made about what to keep, and say it to someone as yours.
cells.core: Some of this you've already weighed and settled. Things kept, things let go, things quietly passed over — and the call was yours each time. You decided the way you decide everything that matters: steadily, testing by what felt right, without announcing a policy. When that's working, it looks like clean keeping — what stays, stays because you meant it, and people can feel the ground under it.\n\nRight now it's running under the hedge. A choice no one knows you made can't be acted on fully — you hold it loosely, revisit it, let it drift. You don't need to declare everything. One kept thing, said out loud. You'll feel the floor under it when it's spoken.
cells.sheetLine: You've already decided what to keep. You haven't claimed it yet.

attempts.check: The record doesn't support the claim that they grew this themselves — 'what transformation grew' may have been done by others, by time, or by accident; I'll say what's been produced, not who produced it. The reader's likely objection is that the crop isn't theirs to gather — I'll keep the harvest as what showed up, not as what they made. The ask survives being wrong: looking over what's actually here is useful whether or not it grew from their own patience. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about 'what you planted' — cut.
